definition: to bring about or initiate (an action, often trouble)
memoryTip: In-stigate: stir the pot — you start the trouble, not stop it.
correctPassage: A single inflammatory post can instigate a wave of online harassment.
wrongPassages: The committee voted to instigate the proposal by tabling it indefinitely.
She hoped to instigate the argument by leaving the room without a word.
They instigated the investigation by shredding every relevant file.

definition: having the opposite of the desired effect
memoryTip: Counter + productive: works against the goal, not toward it.
correctPassage: Harsh punishments can be counterproductive if they drive problems underground.
wrongPassages: The new study schedule proved counterproductive, raising every student's score.
Her calm apology was counterproductive and finally ended the dispute.
Extra practice was counterproductive, so the team improved faster than ever.

definition: the state of keeping careful watch for danger or difficulty
memoryTip: Think night vigil: staying alert and watchful.
correctPassage: Public health depends on continued vigilance against new outbreaks.
wrongPassages: His vigilance showed when he ignored every warning light on the dashboard.
They celebrated their vigilance by leaving the lab unlocked overnight.
She practiced vigilance by skimming the contract and signing immediately.

definition: in a way that seems self-contradictory yet may be true
memoryTip: Paradox: looks impossible, but still holds — 'oddly, both ways true.'
correctPassage: Paradoxically, adding more choices made people less satisfied with their decisions.
wrongPassages: He parked paradoxically, aligning the car perfectly between the lines.
She answered paradoxically, restating the question in clearer words.
The recipe worked paradoxically: follow each step exactly as written.

definition: of great importance or historical significance
memoryTip: Of great moment — a huge, history-making event, not a brief moment.
correctPassage: The signing of the treaty was a momentous event for the region.
wrongPassages: She made a momentous note on a sticky pad and forgot it by lunch.
The momentous delay lasted only three seconds before the train moved.
His momentous choice of socks barely registered with anyone at the party.

definition: not giving way; firm or inflexible
memoryTip: Won't yield — stays rigid, refuses to bend or compromise.
correctPassage: The rock face was unyielding, offering almost no handholds.
wrongPassages: The unyielding foam mattress molded gently to every curve of his back.
Her unyielding stance shifted the moment the first counterargument appeared.
They praised his unyielding schedule, which he rewrote three times a week.

definition: faultless; of the highest standard
memoryTip: Im-peccable (no sin/fault) — zero flaws, spotless.
correctPassage: Her impeccable record made her the natural choice for the appointment.
wrongPassages: His impeccable essay was returned covered in corrections and red ink.
The chef's impeccable sauce separated into oil and grit on the plate.
They hired her for her impeccable attendance: late nearly every morning.

definition: having become rigid in habit or attitude; set in old ways
memoryTip: Os = bone — attitudes harden like bone, stuck and inflexible.
correctPassage: Once-flexible rules had ossified into rigid bureaucracy.
wrongPassages: The startup's culture ossified into open brainstorming and constant change.
She ossified the clay by keeping it damp and workable all afternoon.
Their ossified agenda invited new ideas and reversed old policies weekly.

definition: to publicly declare something or someone to be wrong or evil
memoryTip: De-nounce: publicly name and call out as wrong.
correctPassage: Civic leaders denounce the vandalism as an attack on public memory.
wrongPassages: The mayor rose to denounce the volunteers for their extraordinary service.
Critics denounce the novel as the finest book of the decade.
She denounced the award by thanking the committee and accepting the prize.

definition: to make weak or feeble
memoryTip: De-ability: drain strength until someone can barely function.
correctPassage: A long illness can debilitate even a previously healthy person.
wrongPassages: Daily strength training will debilitate the athletes before championship week.
The restful vacation debilitated her enough to return fully energized.
Extra funding will debilitate the program and expand its reach.

definition: to hinder or impede the progress of
memoryTip: Like a laundry basket in the doorway — blocks the way.
correctPassage: Poor road conditions hamper delivery of supplies to remote villages.
wrongPassages: Clear signage will hamper tourists finding the museum entrance.
The coach's advice only hampered the team's steady improvement.
Extra funding hampered the clinic's ability to hire more nurses.

definition: to appease someone's anger; to soothe or calm
memoryTip: Molli- = soft — soften anger, not harden it.
correctPassage: A partial refund did little to mollify angry customers.
wrongPassages: His sarcastic remark was meant to mollify the already furious crowd.
She tried to mollify the steel beam by heating it until it cracked.
Ignoring every complaint is a reliable way to mollify dissatisfied clients.

definition: empty, bleak, and abandoned in appearance; feeling forsaken
memoryTip: De-solate: a lonely, empty stretch with no life in sight.
correctPassage: After the fire, the once-busy street looked desolate.
wrongPassages: The desolate market thronged with shoppers on a sunny Saturday.
Her desolate garden overflowed with color and visiting neighbors.
They called the packed stadium desolate as the crowd roared.

definition: showing refined taste or careful judgment; selective
memoryTip: Not just bias — a discriminating eye picks quality with care.
correctPassage: A discriminating reader will notice the shift in the author's tone.
wrongPassages: His discriminating palate accepted every cheap wine without a second thought.
She was discriminating in hiring: she interviewed no one and hired at random.
A discriminating collector buys whatever is nearest the door.

definition: acting quickly and rashly, without careful thought
memoryTip: Rides pure impetus — charges ahead before thinking it through.
correctPassage: An impetuous decision to expand too quickly nearly bankrupted the firm.
wrongPassages: Her impetuous plan took six months of research before a single step.
The impetuous driver checked every mirror twice before leaving the curb.
He made an impetuous career choice after carefully listing every risk.

definition: having a dislike or distrust of humankind
memoryTip: Mis + anthropos (human) — distrusts or dislikes people in general.
correctPassage: The character's misanthropic outlook colors every relationship in the novel.
wrongPassages: His misanthropic nature showed in weekly dinners for the whole neighborhood.
The misanthropic hostess thrived on large parties and constant guests.
She was so misanthropic that strangers always felt instantly welcomed.

definition: stubbornly uncooperative or resistant to authority
memoryTip: Re-calcitrant: digs in heels and kicks back — won't cooperate.
correctPassage: Recalcitrant members refused to accept the committee's compromise.
wrongPassages: The recalcitrant intern finished every task early and asked for more.
Recalcitrant voters lined up to support the bill without a single amendment.
Her recalcitrant attitude made her the easiest teammate to manage.

definition: lacking a plan or purpose; jumping from thing to thing
memoryTip: De-sultory leaps: hops around with no clear direction.
correctPassage: Their desultory efforts at reform produced little lasting change.
wrongPassages: His desultory study plan covered every chapter in careful order.
The desultory investigation followed a strict checklist from start to finish.
She gave a desultory presentation that never strayed from the outline.

definition: used for emphasis to mean genuine or true; real
memoryTip: Very + true — a genuine thing: a veritable flood of emails.
correctPassage: The archive is a veritable treasure of primary sources.
wrongPassages: The empty hall was a veritable throng of cheering fans.
Two lukewarm reviews made the film a veritable masterpiece overnight.
His veritable fortune consisted of three dollars and a broken watch.

definition: to faint or nearly faint from extreme emotion
memoryTip: Classic romance trope: so overwhelmed you almost faint.
correctPassage: Fans did not literally swoon, but the concert's energy was overwhelming.
wrongPassages: She managed to swoon through the entire lecture without losing focus.
He will swoon the spreadsheet by sorting every column twice.
The coach told them to swoon harder if they wanted to win the race.
